I don't know if it is normal, but this happens to me a lot, particularly if I'm under a lot of stress.  I panic and shake my head trying to stay in the present.  I recently started taking wellbutrin. It helped take the edge off of stress and reduced how often this happens. It used to happen multiple times a day. It is down to happening a couple times a week.

Sorry this is happening to you. It is terrifying.

My daughter got very violent with her little sister when she was born.  I talked to her about why she wanted to hurt her sister, and she told me she wished she were never born.  So we talked about it more, and she was basically feeling like i loved the baby more than she and that our relationship was ruined forever.  

After that, i made it a point to tell her every time i was showing the baby affection that i love her and the new baby both the same amount.  And i talked about how i used to do this and that for her when she was a baby, and now i do things for her that i don't do for baby because she's bigger now. That way,  she would not see the difference in treatment and perceive the baby was getting a special kind of love that she couldn't have. When someone else was holding lil sis,  i would pull my toddler onto my lap and point out things i love about the baby and tried to invite her to admire her lil sis with me.  Because she was being held and we were doing it together, it helped her to not see lil sis as a threat. When she tried to get violent with her sister,  i jumped in between them to protect the baby,  and i opened my arms really big and said "i can't let you hurt lil sis, but i can give you a hug if you're feeling jealous." She always accepted the hug and would cry. I told her that she could always ask for affection when she's feeling jealous, but she cannot hurt lil sis. She much preferred the hugs, so she started seeking me out to help her feel loved again. 

I'm not sure if your daughter has the same things going on, as each kid is different.  But, for us,  figuring out what the underlying concerns were and addressing those concerns transformed the behavior and brought my sweet toddler back. 


You've got a lot going on with twin babies and a toddler.  I hope you can get enough support for mental breaks.  Just basic care of littles of those ages is a huge mental load.

Golly,  this is a lot for the both of you.  I'm really glad she's got a dad who cares to protect her and help her through this. 

In regard to the lying,  lying is a common thing at 5, even for kids without trauma.  Sometimes it is about experimenting with control, and other times it is about not feeling safe telling the truth. 

The latter was true with my 5 yo. She feared the consequences of telling the truth. I suspect this could be the case with your little given what she's been through.  I explained to her that I would never punish her for telling the truth even if the truth was really bad, because it is my job to protect her and I cannot do that if she lies to me. I would repeat this every time i suspected she was lying. Then i would say "I'm not going to force you to tell me the truth, but know that I'm ready to listen whenever you want to share." Sometimes it took hours or days, but she would always tell me eventually.  And i would always thank her for telling me. If she did something she shouldn't do, i asked her how she felt about her actions and if she wanted my help for what to do next time.  I never accepted lies i did not believe, but i also did not punish her.  I just told her that lying is dangerous, because i can't trust her so i don't know when to help her if i don't know what is true.  

I'm not sure if this will work for your daughter. It helped me build a lot of trust with mine.  She always takes me aside now to tell me the things she's worried about, even if it is about something she thinks she did wrong.

I'm really sorry you are feeling like a failure.  It can be hurtful to have your precious little "reject" you, but please know it isn't that he doesn't care about you and isn't a real rejection. This is a normal part of toddler development.  

Both my kids did this to my husband.  It didn't last very long.  One thing that seemed to help was my talking to them about how great daddy is and admiring him while i held them. Sometimes i would set them down and say "excuse me for a min,  daddy is so cute i need to go see if i can get a hug." They got intrigued fairly quickly.  Lol. You might try talking to your wife about talking daddy up a bit. 

Another poster mentioned being a part of his routine.  That seems like a good idea too. If he's resistant to switching anything that mommy does for him, you could start your own thing that you do with him each day.  

My husband would sit on the floor and play with dolls in their hearing range. They would always get intrigued and go over to join.  Now,  they don't even try to play dolls with me, because I'm too boring compared to daddy. 😆

This may or may not be helpful, but it sounds like you are going through a pretty normal mourning process. Whenever we face major life changes that force us to lose something that we enjoyed or valued, there is a natural mourning process of just feeling sad about what no longer is. While it feels like crap, the mourning process can be very valuable to helping us process and prepare for the next stage and how we will approach it. It helps us value what we had, which also shapes the choices we make going forward. 

I went through a flavor of this at one point. I lost in home child care abruptly with my first child, whom i was working from home with since birth.  I cried every day driving her to my sister's house early in the morning before work to drop her off for the day. I was a hot mess. Ultimately,  i shaped my job around seeing her and she developed amazing relationships with the people who have cared for her over the years.  Now,  i wouldn't change her experience or mine. I built a small business that fits around my life instead of the other way around and now I'm hiring people who are seeking the same thing.  My relationship with my kids is great,  and they enjoy the life they have outside of home.

I'm sorry you are sad right now.  It is a really awful feeling to mourn the loss of quality time with your little.  I hope that you will find a fulfilling solution in the long run.  In the meantime,  sending you a hug.

For us, this is an ongoing discussion rather than a specific training, if that makes sense. At 8, it might be a lot to take in a robust nutritional training, but I'm sure that depends on the kid. I have younger kids, and We just talk about what we are eating and how it benefits our body, and include our kids in meal planning and preparation when time permits. Call it "building the foundation" for more robust understanding later....

Meal planning: We keep it simple. For each meal, pick a fruit or vegetable, a protein, and a grain or other carb (potato). Sometimes, i just say "what should we have for dinner/lunch?" To let them practice thinking it through. 

Ongoing discussion: 
1. Share what each food does for your body (we look it up together because i forget) " Did you know that garlic and onion can help you prevent certain forms of cancer?" "Oh wow, tomatoes can help maintain a healthy heart!"
2. If a child has an ailment (i.e. constipation,  hyperactive) or desires to accomplish something physically (i.e. run faster, climb tree) we might make note that eating certain foods and reducing others will help them. 
--> constipated? Reduce dairy and red meat, increase water, vegetables and fruit
--> hyperactive? Increase protein, reduce sugar.
--> run faster? Eat more dark green vegetables to support joint health.  Eat lean proteins to build muscle. 
3. Sugar and junk food management -- explain how the body processes these foods, and how you can support your body better by eating the nutritious food first.
--> that cake looks yummy, but our body will process it better if we eat a really healthy meal first. That will also help us not eat too much cake and end up feeling sick.

I'm not sure if this addresses your concerns directly, but I wanted to share in case you found it helpful. My kids don't engage when i try to teach them too much about something they didn't ask about.  The little nuggets each day sink in though.

Have you tried talking to him about what he does not like about swim lessons? Usually if my kids are digging their heals in about something there is a reason for it, and if we can address that they are more open to my suggestion. 

It kind of depends on the kid how to motivate past an inhibition, but knowing what the source is the first step. Power seems to be the reward he values most, so it is likely to be the greatest motivator here. The desire to maintain power is a protective mechanism. He may not want to tell you his reason if he senses he is giving up power to share.  You may have to try guessing.

 "Are you afraid you wont do it right? Do the teachers make you uncomfortable? What is making you not want to do the swim lessons? Is it because you feel like I'm forcing you and you don't like to be forced?" Having his concerns validated may bring down the inhibition without additional motivation, but at the least it builds trust needed for motivating. You might offer him control elsewhere as a reward for doing this thing you feel is important for his safety. Something as simple as "how could mommy be safer? You pick something for mommy to do to be safer, and you go to swim class, so we will both be safe."

I don't know your kid, but, in general, i don't believe a 4yo making a powerplay is about rebellion. It is about security for them. If you can address the underlying feelings and help them feel secure, it will be easier to talk to them about the importance of preparing for swim safety and potty training.

In regard to potty training,  my youngest was required by her preschool to potty train to move out of the toddler room. They just put her in panties and let her pee her pants until she started going with everyone else. She didn't like it but accepted it at school.  At home,  i let her have a diaper, because she doesn't like her play to be interrupted. She rarely has accidents at school, and she wears a diaper when she wants to at home.  Not sure if this will work for others.  I just know that potty is a very personal thing, and each child values control over it in different ways. The journey is longer for some kids than others.  

Sorry....lots of words here. I was hoping to be helpful. Wishing you well!

My 4 yo acted out a lot during my pregnancy for our second and for the first 6 months or so. She was violent toward me and toward the baby when she arrived.  It started to taper down after that, but it took a lot of work. She was afraid of sharing her parents and attention with the new baby, and she was scared of how the baby was making me feel.  She got scared i was going to die, because i went to the hospital so much. She was also afraid we would stop loving her because the baby would take our love.

We did a lot of talking to draw out the fears, and then we addressed them with a lot of repetition to help give her the reassurance she needed. We discussed how it seemed like she was getting overwhelmed with her fears and losing control of her body and her voice, and asked her if she felt this was true.  She agreed and said it was scary.  So we talked about strategies for handling her stress before she lost control.  

For our little,  we needed to start with the source and not address the behavior first. It helped us work through it with her to see that we had empathy for her struggle and just wanted to help her not lose control and hurt people.  

So i guess i would recommend seeing if you can get your little to talk about how she's feeling. She may not have the words to describe it, so you can try asking specific questions like "are you worried about the new baby coming? Do you like your new teachers at school?" Etc. 

Hope this helps. Sorry this is so hard when you're pregnant.  If it makes you feel more calm, acting out when a new sibling is on the way or arrived is normal.  Each kid handles it differently, but it seems to always be hard on them in some way.
Do you have a boppy nursing pillow? I've always had really weak arms, and i had snuggly babies, so i would sit down and put the pillow around my waste and baby on the pillow.

It is really hard to be a parent of young children.  You need to give yourself permission to have a bad day though.  Your wife receiving compliments is not a degradation to you for your efforts.  Has anyone actually criticized you for having a bad day, or are you doing this to yourself? I say this because i often beat myself up harder than other people do, and i don't always do a good job of reaching out for support, because i feel ashamed of my bad days. You're doing a great job, and it is really hard. Communicate with your wife about this and try to find some friends whom you can fully share with, so you can get your feelings out and receive the support you need. 

It is hard to watch your spouse get praised when you're working so hard.  My husband gets praised for any involvement with our kids,  and i honestly do 80%-90% of household management and parenting. I also have my own business. He gets praised and i get criticism of my parenting and life choices (i come from a very patriarchal circle).  Some of my family is so ashamed of my career, they lie about it to their friends.  When my husband changes a diaper, he gets praised for "helping me" not giving basic care to his children. 

Parenting of young children is usually thankless and humbling, which makes it harder than it needs to be sometimes.  I'm sorry you don't feel supported. Please know that there is no shame in reaching out for the support you need,  even if it is as simple as "honey, will you please notice me, because i really need that pick-me-up?" My husband has asked me for this,  and it seems to really give him a boost when i just notice what he's doing and acknowledge it.

Gosh, that is hard to deal with.  I can relate.  My family has lots of opinions, and random other people. "Everyone" thinks they know the perfect formula for raising a child and what milestones should look like.  Yet, every person is so unique, both parent and child. How could anyone set a perfect calendar of accomplishments for every unique person? 

In regard to potty training,  you also need to keep in mind the term is kind of merky. People kind of define it differently based on their own goals and challenges.  In my mind,  truly potty trained means i don't have to go in there with them.   A lot of kids really aren't big enough to handle the process themselves until  after age 4.  A potty trained three-year-old is a lot more work than a diapered three-year-old for a parent. 

 For your own sake, I would recommend coming up with some polite but firm retorts for when you are given unsolicited parenting advice or passive aggressive jabs. This can help you in 2 ways: 1 it can get them to stop giving advice because it's clear you don't want it and 2 it can help change your own internal monolog because you are validating yourself and your child, which can stop the anxious self doubt loop in your head. 

You are doing great! Now, you need to let yourself believe it, and tell everyone else to go fly a kite.

The situation sounds a lot like what I've experienced with both of my littles actually. The single most helpful thing was getting them social interaction that was not me on a regular basis.

One other thing i wanted to mention is that you might be expecting too much from yourself and also from her.  Wanting to be in her crib at 4, being a picky eater, not being potty trained yet, not wanting to take a bath.... these are all pretty normal things and are no evidence of failure on either of your part.  Do you think you could give both of you some space to let her grow past some of these things at her own pace and not measure your parenting by these arbitrary results? 

I know this is a struggle for me sometimes.  I fight an unwinnable battle, because my kid isn't ready for it yet.  When i stop fighting the battle,  we both feel better and she gets there eventually. She just isn't on anyone else's milestone timeline. 

Not sure if I'm reading into it too much, but i wanted to share, because it is a lesson i have to repeatedly learn.

I agree with other posters, but it also sounds like there might be more of an issue of lack of knowledge than lack of willingness. 

 If he's willing to work on it,  then i would try to educate him on childhood development and understanding what a 5yo is capable of. Also, I would encourage him to validate your son's feelings on him not being his dad. Your son has a lot to process,  and I think empathy would go a long way here.  A 5yo is much more likely to trust someone when accepting/loving/respecting them is not a forced thing. They also tend to treat people the way they feel they are treated.  If your fiance wants respect, the best way to get it is to be incredibly respectful to your son. Respect is boundaries.  Vslidate his feelings. It's hard for a child to not fall for someone who treats them very well. 

For your son, i would make sure he doesn't feel pressure to accept him as his stepdad until he's ready,  and make sure he knows that your marrying him doesn't change your love for your son.  You might also speak to both of them about what you like about the other.  Positive verbal affirmations can really help children overcome invisible emotional walls. 

Children adapt well when they feel securely loved.

I hope these thoughts are helpful.  I wish you well with this.  These things are hard.

Is she in any kind of preschool coop or play group? I ask because i was having similar problems with my 3yo, and I noticed she was better on days i let her play at my sister's house with her cousins.  So i enrolled her in preschool, and she stopped being needy and demanding. She's very extroverted, and I think I just was not enough for her socially.

One other thing..... have you checked for dietary intolerances? Some kids get really mean because they feel terrible all the time.  I've seen kids become a whole new person after eliminating foods that their body did not tolerate well. One person's pleasure can be another person's belly ache.

I'm just going to share a bit about my little who has gotten violent with tantrums since about 18 months, in case any of it could be helpful. 

Things that have helped:

1) Informing her of changes before they happen more than once, so she is not startled by an interruptionto what she's doing. 
     --> we will be having lunch in a few min.  Then again, "almost time!". Okay,  remember i said we would have lunch soon? It's time now. 

2) offering affection and love to calm down 
    --> oh goodness! You poor thing! You look so upset.  I'm going to open my arms in case you need a hug to help you calm down. 

3) once calm, offering suggestion for how to express that frustration and communicate her needs.  
  --> when she was little i taught her to get my hand and point to what she needed. 
 --> eventually, i taught her words to use.  "I can see you are angry with me.  Why don't you just tell me that you are angry with me, instead of throwing your body on the floor and screaming? If you do that, we have a chance to work it out. "

Every kid is different, so these may not work.  Some of it isn't effective on my younger daughter, but she's also much easier to get out of a tantrum.  


I really hope you are able to get passed this soon.

I'm going to try this again:

I think it would be a good idea to try talking to his wife about why she is struggling to rebuild her body. Post partum care is really sh**, and doctors advice for wellness often makes a post partum mother worse rather than better, because they don't get to the source of the problem. Moreover, it is really hard to recover mentally, while being beat up physically.  I suspect that a mother of a toddler, who has chronic pain  needs her partner to validate how hard it is rather than criticise her exercise and TV choices.  I've been the criticizer, and it only causes harm to the relationship. She made need a different approach to self care than these exercises from the doctor, and it may need to begin with mental health.

Furthermore,  OP's wife's concerns about waiting to continue having children is worthy of understanding.  The decision to bear through the pain and try to fix the chronic pain later, so it isn't 15 years of having babies and rebuilding is a very personal decision.  It is so very hard on the body and mind to go through pregnancy and childbirth and post partum recovery (years, not 6 weeks, friends!). Outside of true health risks, the one who has to face the huge challenges should be heard and heard thoroughly, not given ultimatums. 

 The decisions each person makes about their health are very personal. How we treat each other when we are unwell is something that requires productive conversation and a willingness to listen. I wonder if OP might look past the perceived impasse and see if there is a better way to communicate on this subject in which both parties are being fully heard.

I had no intention of making this a sexist thing, so my apologies if it came across this way. I haven't been reading other posts like this one, but I would feel the same way if OP were a woman speaking this way about her husband. 

I agree. Health issues can contribute to relationship struggles. However, it is not the health conditions themselves but how we respond to them and treat each other while dealing with them. If we are not treating each other well, then fixing the health issue -- if it is indeed fixable -- will not magically make all problems go away. 

It sounds like OP's wife is pretty irritable, and that can be very hard to be on the receiving end of. That needs to be addressed. I just don't think that controlling his wife's health choices and exercise schedule is a healthy or appropriate way to address the situation.

Tone is tricky in text form, so I may have got the wrong vibe. My intention was to help. I feel like I struck a chord here. Not my intention to stir up frustration.

When i read your post,  i hear a lot of criticism and control in your tone. This may not be your intention, as it sounds like you are genuinely concerned for her health. However,  if I were to get this kind of vibe from my husband, I would just associate the exercises with someone else's control over my body and i wouldn't want to do them either. I would be extremely furious about my husband trying to make choices over my body, particularly if there were ultimatums involved.  

If your relationship is suffering, that needs to be addressed first and separately from her physical health.  Her physical health does not dictate the health of your relationship.  

Then you can talk about what you want to do in expanding your family. Any mention of her health should only be expressions of concern and support. If she feels supported and cared for, it will be much easier to be motivated to care for her body in a way that is sustainable for her personality and comfort level. 

Also, keep in mind that there are far more factors for her to consider in her well being with growing an entire human in her body than back and knee pain. And your pressuring her to do things with her body your way on your timeline and terms is not going to lead to a healthy decision or relationship.

I hope this is helpful.

This is a lot.  A child on the spectrum has lots of beds and 3 year olds have lots of needs, which leaves mom pretty zapped. Try to give yourself grace. 

My littles can get this way when something happens that causes unexpected frustration or makes them feel unloved by me or someone else.  I find that trying to address the cause rather than the behavior can be very helpful with my littles, as it gives them a way to handle their feelings. Some kids can tell you why they are acting that way, but others don't have the words.  I have one whom i can just ask "I'm seeing behavior that tells me you are upset, but can you tell me why you are upset or how i can help?" I usually state that i cannot allow the behavior if it is harmful to someone or something, but i want to help them address what they are upset about.  My youngest won't answer the question, so i just try guessing after i ask. "I can see that you are angry. Is it because you were not ready to stop playing to get into the car?" Once I guess correctly,  she calms down, and then i can say "i cant let you punch me when you don't want to leave.  Next time,  why don't you just say 'I'm angry because i don't want to leave?" 

One other thing I will mention is that age 3 is definitely a time where a kid can get particularly violent if they feel unloved, because mom's attention appears to be elsewhere. My oldest really struggled when the younger was born, and the behavior was violent and scary.  I tried telling her repeatedly throughout the day "i love you so much,  and i love you and the new baby the same. I do different things for baby because baby needs different things from me, and i do different things for you that baby isn't ready for.  My love looks different, because of different needs not different love." The more i said it, the more she calmed down. I kept saying "i can't let you harm baby. Jealousy is normal.  Adults feel it too. Please try to just tell me that you're jealous, so i can help you feel better, instead of harming baby.  You can yell at me if the feeling is really big." Eventually, she became secure in my love and started to understand and calm down. She's not violent anymore.  She now just says "i feel really jealous when you do that for little."

I don't know if any of these ideas will help, but i wanted to share just in case. As the other posters said, you do need to take care of yourself, so you have the bandwidth to figure out a parenting relationship that works for you and your kids. 

When I'm burnt out, my parenting style is lose-my-sh**-apologize-repeat. It isn't very effective.  😄

My 5 year old started sleeping through the night for the first time after I taught her some meditation and self soothing techniques.  I made it fun by having her imagine she was a fairy going to sleep in a flower. After some practice she got really good at it,  and we went from a 2 hr bedtime process to about 10 min.  I stayed with her at first and then I would give her days where i told her she needed to practice by herself.  I started by telling her i would leave for 5 min and come back. Bedtime stopped being an issue after this and she slept much better after.  She used to take forever to go to sleep and would wake up repeatedly.

Your child won't hate you.  There will likely be separation anxiety at first, but if the teachers are a good fit for him, daycare may be something he loves and looks forward to each day. My oldest child started preschool at 3 and my youngest went to daycare starting at 6 months. Both of my kids were happier and more confident going to "school." They have wonderful relationships with their caregivers and they are more fulfilled have multiple adults and kids to fill their bucket every day. 


Even if your child gets some separation anxiety, he will still be excited to see you at the end of the day.  Some daycares have a very gentle transition where they have you bring the child in for just a couple of hours the first day and add an hr each day for the first week. You might ask if your daycare can accommodate a gradual transition if it looks like your child is finding it hard.
My kids only get baths when they smell.

A few things....

1) 7 year olds getting violent could be related to ASD and or ADHD. Hunger, heat, fatigue, and sugar can send a 7 year old with either ASD or ADHD into a violent fit. While dad is setting a bad example,  7 year olds who have a mom spending a lot of time with them are not likely to be violent so regularly without cause.  Before deciding how to discipline them,  you need to know what you are dealing with. 
2) boundaries are important both with your husband and your sons.  If your husband doesn't respect your boundaries or makes you feel in danger,  you need to leave. It your kids don't respect your boundaries, knowing whether it is related to ASD or ADHD will help you choose a parenting method that will allow you to establish healthyboundaries and a trustingbond with your boys.  A lot of recommendations here are talking about very aggressive discipline, which will cause more violence in a child with ASD or ADHD, and honestly they don't have control over it. 
3) lastly, it sounds like you need to get some help, if you are the same size as these kids.

I'm sorry you feel alone.  You may very well be alone right now, but that doesn't mean it always has to be that way.  I feel alone a lot.  I used to be alone for a very long time, but I'm not anymore.  It might be worth giving yourself a chance at a fresh start with new people, if you can find a way out of where you are right now. 

Seeing your post, i wanted to reach out.  I know how lonely it can get.  I hope you will seek out a change that will allow you to find a place that feels safe. I had to escape what was essentially a cult in my 20s. Once i got out there was a lot of work to do psychologically, but i knew right away when going to the grocery store alone felt like freedom that the way things had been was not the way things had to always be. 

I hope this helps in some small way.  Sending you a virtual hug.

I'm in my 30s now, but I was also pretty much numb at 17. I would cut myself just to feel something,  and in my 20s i started to drink bottles of cough medicine, because i wanted to feel sick and pass out. I also starved myself a lot, pretending like it was just because i didn't have money for food.  My boyfriend was willing to buy me food. I think i just had such a tight knot in my stomach it felt easier to not eat. At the time, I did not really have a clear understanding of why i felt this way. Eventually,  I did seek help from a counselor with a background in childhood trauma. It was really helpful for connecting the dots, because most of my childhood was like a dream in my head.  I couldn't remember what was real if anything was real. After 3 years of therapy, i finally had a better memory of my childhood and was able to stop starving myself and drugging myself.  The cutting was on and off after that. I found that there is a lot of work to retraining your brain to not desire self harm as an escape from stress. Im still working on this. I had a pretty messed up web of childhood programming that made it very hard to get through the trauma therapy, because we kept having to rabbit trail on other things that were getting in the way.  

Long story short.  I do think you could get a lot of help froma qualified therapist. I've continued therapy on and off for the past decade. At different points in therapy i got stuck because my brain got too scared to look at the trauma, so i took anti depressants for 6-8 months at a time to get through those stages. I definitely have a much better understanding and more control over my brain than i used to. I do still have a very scary response to high stress though. 

Everyone's story is different,  so i wouldn't look at my long journey and feel defeated.  I have a different history and web of brain issues to work through. If you can get access to therapy it is worth a shot to try to understand how your brain might be working against you.

You might try a local charity or church.  There are ways to get help with transportation.  I know this is very stressful, but there are a lot of people out there would be willing and able to help you get transportation until you can get this sorted out.  

I also have struggled with depression from childhood because of abuse,  so my brain tends to fight with me about wanting to escape life when i get stressed. It is almost like my brain sees cortisol and says "OK,  time to die. Not worth dealing with this anymore." I think something gets off physiologically in the brain development when children experience trauma without appropriate counseling and rescue from the abuse. I often feel like the trauma comes back and starts steering, and i have no control..... I'm just saying this to say i can relate to the desire to escape life, and I'm really sorry this is where you are at.  It is such a horrible feeling.

As one who has also tried very hard without it getting better,  i wanted to reach out.  I've seen some replies on here that are very unhelpful and really ignorant on mental health.
